In Module 13 you learned to choose scales and facets, to ask "compared to
what?", and to check that every reader can tell your colors apart. Here you
make those choices on **your own** Fairness and Sports data and publish them,
for the first time, as a report **and** slides: the moves your Challenge
Project reports and presentations need.

## What you'll hand in

1. A **report page** and a **slides page**, both published on your site.
2. Their **two links**, in Blackboard.
3. Both are built from **one script**: you edit the code once, and both
   pages show it.

### Two milestones

| Milestone | When | What | Graded? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Draft | See Blackboard | Tasks 0–5 done with checks passing; report published with your WRITE answers; slides as a first draft | No: you get feedback |
| Final | See Blackboard (end of Module 14) | Report and slides revised with Module 14's ideas, plus a revision log | Yes: the rubric |

Both go to the same Blackboard assignment (see **Finish and submit**). See
Blackboard for the due date and time.

## Do each task the same way (the loop)

1. **Script:** go to the task's section in `scripts/gp13_scales_facets.R`,
   fill in the code (the lines marked **YOUR TURN**), and run it, until the
   check says **PASS**. A **TO DO** says what to fix.
2. **Report:** open `reports/gp13_report.qmd`, find the same task, and write
   under **WRITE**.
3. **Render** the report and look at the task.
4. **Commit and push** whenever you stop.

Part A (Fairness) has more help; Part B (Sports) asks you to write more of
the code yourself, using Part A as your model. The **Reference** section at
the end of this page has the project map, the words you'll see, and ideas
for your columns.

**Stuck?** In order: the check's TO DO message; the matching practice
exercise ([practice page](practice.qmd){target="_blank"}, with solutions);
the class scripts (`live/module13_session1.R`, `live/module13_session2.R` in
your `module-13-scales-facets` project); a classmate; office hours or email.
After a restart ("object not found"), run the script from the top
(Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).

### Task 1 · Label it {#task-1}

**Goal:** Make your plot readable without your code.

**Practice first:** [D1 · Label it](practice.qmd#d1-label-it){target="_blank"}

| Step | What you do | How it's checked |
|---|---|---|
| A1 · Fairness | Paste your Module 12 A0 lines as `a_data` and your A1 plot as `a1_base`. In `labs()`: a title that states what the plot shows, a subtitle (the data and its n), axis titles with units, a legend title. Percent labels on the rate axis | The script (PASS / TO DO) |
| B1 · Sports | The same on a Sports plot of your choice: `b_data`, `b1_base`, `b1` | The script (PASS / TO DO) |
| Write (report) | Which label you changed most, and why. Could a reader understand the plot without you there? | Your instructor reads it (counts under Choices) |

### Task 2 · Choose a scale {#task-2}

**Goal:** Choose the scale that fits your data, and say why.

**Practice first:** [D2 · Choose a scale](practice.qmd#d2-choose-a-scale){target="_blank"}
and [D3 · The Lie Factor](practice.qmd#d3-the-lie-factor){target="_blank"}

| Step | What you do | How it's checked |
|---|---|---|
| A2 · Fairness | `a2`: a log scale for a skewed column, or percent labels for a share. A log scale can't show 0 or negative values: keep only values above 0 and count them. One sentence in `a2_reason` | The script (PASS / TO DO) |
| B2 · Sports | The same with a Sports column: `b2`, `b2_reason` | The script (PASS / TO DO) |
| Write (report) | Which scale, and why; what a reader sees with it; how many values were removed, if any | Your instructor reads it (counts under Choices) |

### Task 3 · Facet it: fixed or free {#task-3}

**Goal:** Split one plot into panels, and choose fixed or free axes for the
reader.

**Practice first:** [D4 · Fixed or free panels](practice.qmd#d4-fixed-or-free-panels){target="_blank"}
and [D5 · Two facets at once](practice.qmd#d5-two-facets-at-once-sex-and-species){target="_blank"}

| Step | What you do | How it's checked |
|---|---|---|
| A3 · Fairness | `a3_fixed` and `a3_free`: your A1 rates in panels by a second column, each panel's n in its label. Then `a3_choice` (`"fixed"` or `"free_y"`) and `a3_reason` | The script (PASS / TO DO) |
| B3 · Sports | The same, in panels by a group or a year: `b3_fixed`, `b3_free`, `b3_choice`, `b3_reason` | The script (PASS / TO DO) |
| Write (report) | Fixed or free? What the reader gains and loses; which panels are small, with their n. Differences, not causes | Your instructor reads it (counts under Choices and Interpretation) |

### Task 4 · Compared to what? {#task-4}

**Goal:** Show whether a difference between two groups is large or small,
compared to the spread of the individuals and to how much a mean can move.

**Practice first:** [D6 · Uncertainty clouds](practice.qmd#d6-uncertainty-clouds){target="_blank"}

| Step | What you do | How it's checked |
|---|---|---|
| A4 · Fairness | Choose a numeric column (e.g., hours per week, age, number of medications), not the yes/no outcome, and two groups. `make_clouds()` (prepared in Section 0) adds 200 resampled means to the individual values. Draw `a4` with `facet_wrap(~ kind)` and the same axes in both panels | The script (PASS / TO DO): panels by `kind`, fixed axes, exactly two groups |
| B4 · Sports | The same with a Sports numeric column: `b4_clouds`, `b4` | The script (PASS / TO DO) |
| Write (report) | Do the clouds overlap? What does that say about individuals versus the group means? | Your instructor reads it (counts under Choices and Interpretation) |

### Task 5 · Color for every reader {#task-5}

**Goal:** Use colors every reader can tell apart, and never color alone.

**Practice first:** [D7 · Color for every reader](practice.qmd#d7-color-for-every-reader){target="_blank"}
(and the redundant cue in [D9](practice.qmd#d9-more-scale-choices-size-gray-fills-redundant-cues){target="_blank"})

| Step | What you do | How it's checked |
|---|---|---|
| A5 · Fairness | Map a column with few categories (2 to 4) to `color` or `fill`, with `scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8)` (or `scale_color_viridis_d()`). Run `color_check(a5)`. Add a second cue: direct labels (`geom_text()` or `geom_label()`), panels, or the same column on x or y | The script (PASS / TO DO): each category its own color, at least 20 in all three rows, a second cue |
| B5 · Sports | The same with a Sports column (or one you make): `b5` | The script (PASS / TO DO) |
| Explain your colors (in the report) | Say which column you colored by and why. If your first choice failed the color check, say what you changed: fewer categories, grouping rare ones, or panels. Then look at your simulated plot: can you still tell the categories apart? | Your instructor reads it (counts under Choices) |

**What the numbers mean.** `color_check()` simulates how your colors look to
readers with three types of color blindness, then measures how far apart the
two closest colors are (a standard color difference, delta E). Bigger is
easier to tell apart; 20 is our course's line for clearly different. The
three rows are red-green (deuteranopia), red-green (protanopia) and
**blue-yellow (approximate)**. Below 20? Choose a column with fewer
categories, group rare ones with care (keep small groups visible and say
so), or use panels.

**See it, not only the numbers.** `simulate_plot()` redraws your plot in the
same simulated colors. Your report shows your plot and the red-green
(deuteranopia) version side by side, and the other two views below them.

The red-green simulations come from a validated model; the blue-yellow one
is an approximation. Machado, G. M., Oliveira, M. M., & Fernandes, L. A. F.
(2009). A physiologically-based model for simulation of color vision
deficiency. *IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics,
15*(6), 1291–1298. <https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2009.113>

## Build your slides (task 6) {#task-6}

**Goal:** Tell one finding to an audience, in at least 4–5 slides.

**Practice first:** [D8 · Check a deck](practice.qmd#d8-check-a-deck){target="_blank"}

| Step | What you do | How it's checked |
|---|---|---|
| Slides | Open `presentations/gp13_slides.qmd`. Replace each prompt with your own words (the checklist below). Choose plots from Part A, Part B or both by chunk name: copy a figure chunk and change `ref.label` (`a1` … `a5`, `a3-chosen`, `b1` … `b5`). Render | Your instructor reads it (counts under Interpretation and Innovation and creativity) |
| Write (report) | "One thing I tried in my slides, and why": one idea of your own (an angle, a comparison, an order, an annotation) and how it helps a reader | Your instructor reads it (counts under Innovation and creativity) |

No code goes in the slides: a plot appears by naming its chunk from the
script. The headline slide shows your A3 plot, the version you chose.

- [ ] **Title** (in the YAML at the top): what is this about, and who made
  it?
- [ ] **Question:** one sentence, naming the groups you compare.
- [ ] **Data:** where it's from, what one row is, how many rows.
- [ ] **Your headline:** the finding in one sentence, then the figure.
- [ ] **What it shows, and its limits:** differences, not causes;
  provenance, small groups, what the data can't tell us.
- [ ] **Why it matters** (final version only): one or two sentences on
  what your finding means for the reader.
- [ ] **Sources and AI use:** the data citation; one line on AI use (or
  "AI use: none.").

Elements can share a slide. **At least 4–5 slides; more are welcome.** For a
model, open the **Example** menu on your site: the penguins report and the
penguins slides. **Speaker notes are public** on the web: leave them out.

## Finish and submit

**Final checklist** (draft and final):

- [ ] Every check says **PASS** in the Checks table at the end of your
  report (ten checks; A0 is a reminder).
- [ ] Both pages render, and both links open in a private (incognito)
  window.
- [ ] Each plot has a one-sentence `fig-alt` that describes **your** plot.
- [ ] Small groups are shown, with their n, not dropped: under-represented is
  not unimportant.
- [ ] No private person's name in your report or slides (no name, bib, team
  or judge column in a plot, table or slide).
- [ ] One line on AI use in your report (AI use section) and on your last
  slide, for example "AI use: I used [tool] to [what for]." or "AI use:
  none."
- [ ] **Final version only:** the **Revision log** in your report: three to five
  changes, each with what changed, why, and which idea from Module 14 it
  uses.
- [ ] **Final version only:** your "why it matters" line in your slides (under
  "What it shows, and its limits") and in your report: one or two
  sentences on what your finding means for the reader.

**Submitting.** Submit in the designated Blackboard assignment **"Guided
Project: Scales and Facets"**, the same assignment both times (up to 5
attempts). Your links stay the same; pushing updates the pages. Your last
attempt before the final deadline is the one graded.

1. **Type in the text box** your two links, your AI log and the attestation
   (copy the template in **Reference**, AI log template). For the final,
   update the log.
2. **Upload copies of all your AI conversations** as .txt, PDF or Word, saved
   on your own computer, with personal information removed. **Never put the
   log or the conversations in your Posit Cloud project:** everything there
   is pushed to the public site. Blackboard doesn't accept `.html`.
3. **If pushing failed** (token, Pages not updating): zip
   `docs/reports/gp13_report.html` and `docs/presentations/gp13_slides.html`
   (each is one file, plots included), attach the zip, and say what went

## Reference

### Project map

Your `cis-3901-projects` project, with the files GP13 uses. Your project may
have a few more.

```default
cis-3901-projects/
├── data/
│   ├── fairness.csv           GP13 reads this (Section 0 moves it here)
│   ├── sports.csv             GP13 reads this
│   ├── example/penguins.csv   the penguins example's data
│   ├── fairness/              the messy Tidy Data package: not used here
│   ├── tidy/                  your tidy files from Modules 10–11 (GP12 read fairness.csv here)
│   └── sports/                your SCORE downloads (GP12 read sports.csv here)
├── scripts/
│   ├── gp13_scales_facets.R   you edit the code here
│   ├── gp12_stats_coords.R    Module 12 (finished)
│   └── 01_tidy_fairness.R, 02_tidy_sports.R   Modules 10–11
├── reports/
│   ├── gp13_report.qmd        reads the GP13 script's chunks
│   └── gp12_report.qmd, fairness_report.qmd, sports_report.qmd
├── presentations/

│   └── fairness_slides.qmd, sports_slides.qmd
```

What reads what: the script reads `data/fairness.csv` and `data/sports.csv`.
The report and the slides read the script's chunks. **Render** writes
`docs/reports/gp13_report.html` and `docs/presentations/gp13_slides.html`.
After a push, GitHub Pages publishes `docs/`.

### One script, two outputs

```default
scripts/gp13_scales_facets.R   ← you edit the code here
        │ chunks read by name
        ├──► reports/gp13_report.qmd        → your report page
        └──► presentations/gp13_slides.qmd  → your slides page
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Edit the code in the script. The report and the slides only read it.

Your words (findings, headlines, limits) live in the report and the slides.
:::

Each chunk in the script starts with a label line such as `## ---- a1 ----`.
The report and the slides call the same chunks by name (with
`knitr::read_chunk()`), so when you change a plot in the script and render,
both pages show the new plot. Rendering the report doesn't render the
slides: render both before you push.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake

If you type code into a chunk in the report or the slides, it is ignored:
on render, that chunk runs the script's code instead. Your change doesn't
show on the page, and the checks don't see it. A new code chunk you add does
run, but only on that page, so your report, slides and script no longer
match. Keep those chunks empty and fix the code in the script.
:::

### Words you'll see

- **Script:** a file of R code you run a few lines at a time
  (Ctrl/Cmd + Enter). Here, `scripts/gp13_scales_facets.R` holds all the
  code.
- **Chunk:** a block of code. In the script, the lines from one label line
  to the next; in a `.qmd` file, a block that starts with ```` ```{r} ````.
- **Chunk label:** a chunk's name. In the script it's a line such as
  `## ---- a1 ----`; the report and the slides find the code by that name.
- **Quarto:** the program that turns a `.qmd` file into a web page or slides.
- **`.qmd` file:** a Quarto document: your words plus code chunks. Here,
  `reports/gp13_report.qmd` and `presentations/gp13_slides.qmd`.
- **knitr:** the R package that runs a `.qmd` file's code chunks and puts
  their output into the document.
- **Render:** the Render button. knitr runs the code chunks, then Quarto
  builds the page or the slides. (R Markdown called this Knit.) It renders
  only the file that is open.
- **Report:** the web page built from `gp13_report.qmd`: code, output and
  your findings.
- **Slides:** the deck built from `gp13_slides.qmd` (revealjs: slides that
  open in a web browser; the arrow keys move between them).
- **`knitr::read_chunk()`:** the line near the top of the report and the
  slides that reads the script's chunks, so a chunk named `a1` there runs
  the script's `a1` code.
- **Output:** what code produces: a plot, a table, a PASS or TO DO line.
  Render's output is an HTML file in `docs/`.
- **Commit:** saves a snapshot of the files you ticked, with a message, in
  your project's history (Git tab).
- **Push:** sends your commits to your repository on GitHub (with your
  token).
- **GitHub Pages:** the GitHub service that publishes your repository's
  `docs/` folder as your website, a minute or two after a push.
- **URL:** a web address. Your two pages' URLs are the links you submit.

### Ideas for your columns

Starting points; check them in the column list Section 0 prints for your own
file (name, type, how many different values). Each dataset gets the same kind
of hint: task 2 (a skewed column, or a share for percent labels), task 3
(panels: a group or a year), task 4 (two groups and a numeric column) and
task 5 (a column with 2 to 4 categories, or how to make one). Small groups
stay in your plots, with their n.

**Fairness**

- **Adult:** task 2 `capital_gain` (most are 0: keep values above 0 with
  `filter()` and say how many); task 3 `race`; task 4 `hours_per_week` (or
  `age`) by `sex`; task 5 `sex` or `income`.
- **ACS Income NC:** task 2 `income`; task 3 `sex` or `marital_status`;
  task 4 `hours_per_week` by `sex`; task 5 `sex`.
- **Diabetes Hospital:** task 2 a share with percent labels (readmission);
  task 3 `gender` (one panel has n = 2: keep it) or `race`; task 4
  `num_medications` by `gender`, Female and Male (Unknown/Invalid, n = 2, is
  too small for a cloud: say so); task 5 `age`.
- **Credit Card:** task 2 `limit_bal`; task 3 `sex` or `marriage`; task 4
  `age` (or `limit_bal`) by `sex`; task 5 `sex`, or `marriage` (two small
  groups).

**Sports**

- **WNBA:** task 2 a share of wins with percent labels; task 3
  `season_type` (2 regular season, 3 playoffs: name them with `if_else()`);
  task 4 make a number first: each team's share of wins in a season, at
  home and away (`group_by()` team, `season` and `team_home_away`, then
  `summarize()`), then the clouds by `team_home_away`; task 5
  `team_home_away`.
- **NFL Draft Combine:** task 2 a share picked in round 1; task 3 make a
  group from `Round` (empty = not drafted) with `if_else()`; task 4 `forty`
  for drafted and not drafted; task 5 that group.
- **Boston Marathon:** task 2 a share finishing under a time you choose,
  from `finish_net_minutes`; task 3 `gender` or `age_group` (80+ has n = 5:
  keep it); task 4 `finish_net_minutes` by `gender`; task 5 `gender`. Never
  use `name`, `bib_number` or `team`.
- **Setka Cup:** task 2 a share of home wins; task 3 make a group from
  `HomeWinner` with `if_else()`; task 4 the points in game 1
  (`P1_G1 + P2_G1`) by who won the match (`HomeWinner`); task 5 sets played,
  `Sets_P1` plus `Sets_P2`, with `factor()`.
- **Sumo:** task 2 a share of winning records; task 3 make a weight band
  from `weight_kg` with `if_else()`; task 4 `weight_kg` for two rank letters
  from `Rank` with `str_sub()` (M and J: J has only 28 records, so its cloud
  of means is wide); task 5 the weight band, or `Rank`'s first letter with
  `fct_lump_n()` (say what you combined).
- **MLB pitches:** task 2 a share of strikes; task 3 `player_name`; task 4
  `release_speed` for balls and strikes (`result` B and S); task 5 `result`
  (B, S, X).
- **Powerlifting:** task 2 a share of first places, from `Place`; task 3 two
  periods from `Date` with `year()` and `if_else()` (early years are small);
  task 4 `TotalKg` for those two periods; task 5 a bodyweight band from
  `BodyweightKg` with `cut()` (a few missing: `drop_na()`). Never use
  `Name`.
- **WTA Grand Slam:** task 2 `winner_rank` (a few missing: `drop_na()`);
  task 3 a year from `tourney_date` with `str_sub()`; task 4 `minutes` on
  Hard and Clay courts (`surface`; matches without minutes are left out);
  task 5 `surface`.
- **MMA fight decisions:** task 2 a share where all judges agree; task 3 a
  year from `date` with `year()` (21 years: two periods read better); task 4
  a judge's margin, `abs(judge1_margin)`, for 3- and 5-round fights
  (`rounds`; the 24 twelve-round fights left out); task 5 `result_type`.
  Never use the `judge1`–`judge3` columns.

### Grading (percentage ranges in the rubric)

The rubric grades the final. The draft gets feedback only.

**Levels (all criteria):** Exemplary 90–100% · Proficient 80–89% · Developing
65–79% · Beginning 1–64% · No Response 0%.

| Criterion | Weight | Looks at |
|---|---|---|
| Code and checks: script runs; checks pass; report and slides render and are published | 35% | Your code and output, Checks table, both pages |
| Choices: labels, scale, fixed or free, the clouds' groups and column, colors and categories, each with a reason; the revision log | 25% | Your writing, both datasets |
| Interpretation: findings, limits, small groups, no causal claims | 20% | Your writing and slides |
| Innovation and creativity (slides) | 10% | Your slides, and "One thing I tried in my slides, and why" |
| AI disclosure | 10% | AI use line in your report and slides, AI log typed in Blackboard (or the no-AI statement), and copies of all AI conversations uploaded in Blackboard |

**Innovation and creativity (slides):**

- **Exemplary (90–100%):** every minimum element, plus an idea of your own
  (an angle, a comparison, an order, an annotation) that helps the reader
  see the finding.
- **Proficient (80–89%):** every minimum element, close to the penguins
  example.
- **Developing (65–79%):** the example's structure with new plots dropped
  in; default or topic-only titles.
- **Beginning (1–64%):** the slides don't convey a finding.

Decoration doesn't count. An idea that distorts the data or breaks the color
rules earns no credit. More slides aren't more credit. Artistic skill isn't
graded.

### AI use (Level 2) and the AI log template

You may use AI to explain code or errors. Write your own sentences in the
report and the slides.

- **Public:** one line in your report's **AI use** section and on your last
  slide, for example "AI use: I used [tool] to [what for]." or "AI use:
  none."
- **In Blackboard (private):** your AI log or the no-AI statement, the
  attestation, and copies of all your AI conversations.

Copy this into the Blackboard text box:

```default
Report: https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/cis-3901-projects/reports/gp13_report.html
Slides: https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/cis-3901-projects/presentations/gp13_slides.html

AI log
Use 1 – Tool: ___ | What I used it for: ___ | What I changed or checked, and why: ___
Use 2 – Tool: ___ | What I used it for: ___ | What I changed or checked, and why: ___
(add a line per use; upload a copy of every conversation)

OR: I did not use AI for this project. How I worked through problems: ___

Attestation: This log lists every use of AI in this project.
```
